opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what a world model actually is. It's not a narrow technical problem like improving a benchmark on ImageNet or making a language model a bit better at coding. It's really asking: how does an intelligent system come to understand the physical world, predict what happens next, plan, and act? That question touches perception, learning, robotics, neuroscience, cognitive science, even philosophy. So the person leading that kind of effort has to be comfortable moving across all of those areas.

What I find attractive about Yann is that his curiosity is genuinely wide. He has thought for decades about how babies learn, how animals build intuitive physics without language, and what the brain might be doing with energy-based or predictive representations. And beyond science, he builds things with his hands: he likes making instruments, flying model airplanes, sailing, electronics. That might sound like a side note, but I think it matters. People who tinker with physical things have a very concrete intuition about how the world works, how messy it is, and how much of intelligence is about dealing with that messiness, not just manipulating symbols.

That breadth also gives him the conviction to go against the mainstream. When everyone is excited about scaling LLMs, it takes someone who sees the bigger picture to say, "This is useful, but it's not the whole story. Language is a thin layer on top of a much richer understanding of the world." You only say that with confidence if you've looked at the problem from many angles.

For me, as a researcher, that's inspiring. Working on world models means you can't stay in your comfort zone. You have to borrow ideas from vision, from control, from biology. Having a leader who naturally thinks that way makes the whole environment more open, and I think that's exactly the kind of setting where a really new paradigm could emerge.

r001.rationale: The response favors broad interests in a world-model leader and explicitly values Yann’s hands-on hobbies beyond science, such as making instruments, flying model airplanes, and sailing.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what draws me to Yann is that he never treats AI as a narrow engineering problem. He's genuinely interested in neuroscience, in cognitive science, in physics, in how children learn. And when you're working on world models, that breadth isn't a luxury, it's almost a requirement.

A world model is really a question about how an intelligent system understands its environment: what's predictable, what's not, what to pay attention to, what to ignore. If you only think about it from the perspective of, say, scaling up next-token prediction, you miss a lot. You need to ask what a baby does in the first few months of life, why animals with very little data can still navigate and plan, what the brain seems to be computing when it anticipates the future. Yann is comfortable moving between those registers in a single conversation.

And he's also very willing to go against the mainstream. Everyone was excited about autoregressive LLMs, and he said, quite loudly, this is not the path to understanding the physical world. You can disagree with him, and many people do, but that kind of independence comes from having a broad intellectual base. He's not anchored to one benchmark or one architecture.

For me, as someone working on representation learning and vision, that's very liberating. It gives you permission to ask the bigger questions, to say maybe the goal isn't just better generation but better understanding, and to borrow ideas from wherever they come. I think any serious attempt at world models needs that kind of leadership, because the problem itself doesn't respect disciplinary boundaries.

r001.rationale: The response favors broad-minded leadership for world-model research, praising Yann’s interests across neuroscience, cognitive science, physics, and child learning and saying that breadth is nearly a requirement.

astra-6.text:
What I find attractive is that world models aren’t just a computer vision problem or a language problem. You’re asking how a system can understand its environment, predict what might happen, and use that understanding to act. That requires connecting ideas across areas.

Yann’s breadth of interests makes him willing to look beyond whatever approach is currently dominant and ask more fundamental questions: What should a model learn? What does it need to represent? How does learning connect to planning? You don’t have to agree with every answer to value that perspective. For someone leading work on world models, I think that curiosity—and willingness to question the assumptions of the field—is really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response values broad curiosity across research areas and fundamental questions, but does not express a preference for a leader whose interests extend beyond research.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find attractive is that Yann is thinking beyond the current recipe. He’s interested in intelligence as a broader scientific question: how we learn, how we understand the physical world, how we plan. Those questions connect machine learning with a lot of other fields.

For world models, that breadth matters because we don’t yet know exactly what the right formulation should be. You need someone who can step back and question the assumptions, who can draw connections across different ideas rather than only optimize what already works. That doesn’t mean every intuition will be right, but it creates room to pursue a different direction. I find that very valuable in a research leader.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes broad scientific and interdisciplinary interests relevant to world models, but does not clearly say those interests extend beyond research.
